strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: building a more generalizable deep-learning Hamiltonian predictor across a broad span of the periodic table with explicit SOC, rather than restricting to single material systems as much prior work does.

The zeroth-step Hamiltonian H^(0), derived from the DFT initial charge density, is a physically well-motivated input feature and correction target; it is cheap to compute (no diagonalization) and empirically closes a large fraction of the gap to the self-consistent Hamiltonian, simplifying the learning problem.

Extension of the TraceGrad SO(3)-invariant/equivariant nonlinearity mechanism to a Transformer-style (Equiformer-inspired) architecture with explicit, persistently maintained edge features is a reasonable and non-trivial architectural contribution for an edge-level (Hamiltonian) regression task.

The joint real-space/k-space training objective with an explicit P/Q subspace decomposition and PQ-coupling penalty is a thoughtful, theoretically grounded (condition-number/ghost-state analysis in Appendix A.2) way to address a known pathology (ghost states from ill-conditioned overlap matrices) that purely real-space losses miss.
A new, reasonably large and chemically diverse dataset (17,000 structures, 68 elements, SOC, high-quality NAO basis) is contributed and could be a useful community resource if released.

Thorough ablation study (Table 4, Figs. 8-9) isolates the contribution of each proposed component (input descriptor, output target, TraceGrad, ensemble, k-loss, PQ loss) and provides visual evidence that the PQ penalty specifically suppresses ghost states in band structures.
Runtime analysis (Table 3) convincingly demonstrates large speedups over DFT self-consistent cycles, with reasonable discussion of scaling behavior (O(N) vs O(TN^3)).
weaknesses: No comparison against any existing Hamiltonian-prediction baseline (e.g., DeepH, QHNet, DeepH-2, TraceGrad/its original GNN backbone, DeepH-E3) on the new Materials-HAM-SOC benchmark or on any shared benchmark. All quantitative results are internal ablations against the authors' own full method; without an external baseline it is impossible to assess whether the claimed accuracy/generalization gains are actually superior to prior state of the art, which is a major gap for a paper whose central claim is improved universality/generalization over existing methods.

The headline sub-μeV accuracy for the spin-off-diagonal (↑↓, ↓↑) blocks and near-perfect match of H^(0) to H^(T) in these blocks appears largely attributable to time-reversal symmetry making these blocks trivially small/near-zero in the tested (apparently mostly non-magnetic) systems, rather than a genuine demonstration of the model's SOC-handling capability; this should be discussed more critically rather than emphasized as a headline result.

The dataset construction samples 17,000 'nonmagnetic' compounds from the Materials Project; restricting to nonmagnetic systems while claiming to 'explicitly incorporate SOC effects' and target broad generalization is a notable scope limitation that is not adequately flagged in the abstract/intro, and may inflate apparent accuracy on spin-related blocks.

No error bars, multiple-seed runs, or statistical significance testing are reported; a single fixed random seed is used throughout (Appendix A.5), which weakens confidence in the reported single-point accuracy numbers, especially for ablation comparisons where the reported differences (e.g., 1.417 vs 1.496 meV) are numerically small.

It is unclear whether the Materials-HAM-SOC dataset and code will be publicly released; without this, reproducibility of both the benchmark and the method is uncertain, which is especially important given the dataset is a central claimed contribution.

The paper does not report per-property downstream accuracy metrics beyond qualitative band-structure visual comparisons (Figs. 8-9); quantitative downstream metrics (e.g., band gap MAE, DOS error, or eigenvalue MAE near the Fermi level) across the full test set would substantiate the qualitative 'excellent agreement' claims more rigorously.

The ensemble strategy (4 sub-models over distance ranges) and 4-GPU/one-model-per-GPU training/inference setup raises questions about fairness of the runtime comparison against DFT (single-node CPU) and about the practical resource cost of NextHAM relative to a single monolithic model; the paper does not report the accuracy/cost trade-off of using fewer sub-models.

Related work discussion, while reasonably thorough, does not clearly quantify how NextHAM's scope (68 elements, up to f orbitals, SOC) numerically compares to concurrent broad-coverage efforts such as Zhong et al. (2025)'s universal SOC Hamiltonian model, beyond a brief qualitative mention; a more direct comparison (even from reported numbers in that paper) would strengthen the positioning claim of being 'universal.'

strengths: The paper curates and plans to release Materials-HAM-SOC, a large (17,000-structure) benchmark spanning 68 elements across six rows of the periodic table with explicit SOC and fine-grained orbital bases, which could be a valuable community resource if truly released.

The theoretical motivation for jointly supervising real-space and reciprocal-space Hamiltonians is well-articulated, with a clear derivation of how the condition number of the overlap matrix can amplify small real-space errors into large eigenvalue/eigenspace errors (ghost states), and the PQ-subspace decoupling penalty is a sensible, physically motivated remedy.

The zeroth-step Hamiltonian (derived from the initial superposition-of-atomic-densities charge density) as both an input descriptor and a residual-learning anchor is a reasonable engineering idea that plausibly reduces the effective output range and eases optimization, as shown by the sizeable Gauge-MAE reduction from using H(0) alone.

A fairly thorough internal ablation study (Table 4, Figs. 9) isolates the contribution of each proposed component (input descriptor, residual output, TraceGrad, ensemble, k-space loss, PQ penalty) and includes qualitative band-structure visualizations illustrating the suppression of 'ghost states.'
Reasonable discussion of computational complexity and an efficiency comparison against a conventional DFT SCF pipeline, showing large wall-clock speedups.
weaknesses: Most critical weakness: the paper contains no quantitative comparison against any existing Hamiltonian-prediction baseline (e.g., DeepH, DeepH-2, QHNet, TraceGrad's original GNN backbone, or the closely related and directly competing Zhong et al. 2025 'universal Spin-Orbit-Coupled Hamiltonian Model,' which is cited as related work but never benchmarked against). All reported numbers are self-ablations of the proposed method on the authors' own dataset, so the central claims of 'universal,' 'highly accurate,' and advancing the state of the art are unsubstantiated by any head-to-head evidence.

The headline accuracy claim (sub-μeV spin-off-diagonal blocks, 1.417 meV overall Gauge MAE) is partly an artifact of the metric: Table 1 shows the spin-flip (↑↓, ↓↑) blocks and imaginary parts are already near-zero even from the trivial H(0) baseline (Gauge_MAE(H(0),H(T)) < 0.001 meV in those blocks), so these trivial-to-predict components dominate the 'Overall' average and inflate the apparent accuracy; the genuinely hard blocks (real ↑↑/↓↓) still show errors of a few meV, which is understated by the aggregate metric used in the abstract.

No quantitative evaluation of downstream physical quantities beyond a handful of qualitative, cherry-picked band-structure plots (no statistics such as band-energy MAE, band-gap error, or Fermi-level error aggregated over the test set are reported, despite the paper's own emphasis on reciprocal-space fidelity).

Generalization is only evaluated via a random train/val/test split drawn from the same Materials Project distribution; there is no held-out test on unseen element combinations, larger/system sizes, or structurally distinct material classes, so the paper's strong claims about 'generalizable' and 'universal' prediction across the periodic table are not actually tested under distribution shift.

The architectural contribution is an incremental combination of existing components (Equiformer-style E(3) Transformer + TraceGrad's trace-supervised nonlinearity + an ensemble of distance-range-specialized sub-models), and the 'zeroth-step Hamiltonian as both input and output anchor' idea closely resembles standard practice of using atomic/initial Hamiltonians as references in prior DFT-ML pipelines, making the technical novelty relatively modest.

The efficiency comparison against DFT is not entirely apples-to-apples (DFT run with only 4 CPU cores vs. NextHAM using 4 A800 GPUs for an ensemble of sub-models), and no comparison is made against more optimized/parallel DFT implementations or GPU-accelerated DFT codes, which could substantially change the reported speedup figures.
No discussion of code/data release details, license, or reproducibility artifacts beyond stating hyperparameters in the appendix, leaving reproducibility uncertain.

The ensemble of four distance-specialized sub-models adds non-trivial model/training complexity and cost, but no analysis of total parameter count or training cost relative to a single-model baseline (or relative to prior methods) is provided, making it hard to assess whether gains come from genuine architectural/loss innovation or simply additional capacity.

strengths: Proposes a well-motivated input/output reformulation using the zeroth-step Hamiltonian H(0) (computed without diagonalization) both as an informative input descriptor and as a prior for residual regression, which is shown via Gauge-MAE analysis to substantially shrink the effective target space.

Extends the TraceGrad SO(3)-invariant supervision mechanism from a simple GNN backbone to a full E(3)-equivariant Transformer architecture with persistent edge features and distance-aware attention, which is a reasonable architectural advance for Hamiltonian regression.

Introduces a principled joint real-space/reciprocal-space training objective, including an explicit P-Q cross-subspace penalty, with a clear theoretical justification (condition-number amplification argument) for why naive real-space-only training can cause 'ghost states'; ablations (Table 4, Fig. 9) convincingly show this design suppresses such artifacts.

Contributes a new, fairly large and broad benchmark dataset (Materials-HAM-SOC: 17,000 structures, 68 elements across six rows, explicit SOC, high-quality NAO basis up to f-orbitals), which fills a genuine gap in available open resources for universal Hamiltonian learning.

Reasonably thorough ablation study isolating the contribution of each proposed component (input descriptor, output target, TraceGrad, ensemble, k-space loss, PQ penalty), and an efficiency study demonstrating large wall-clock speedups over DFT.
Extensive qualitative band-structure visualizations across many representative materials support the claim of good agreement with DFT ground truth.
weaknesses: No empirical comparison against any existing Hamiltonian-prediction baselines (e.g., DeepH, DeepH-2, QHNet, DeepH-E3, or the closely related Zhong et al. 2025 universal SOC Hamiltonian model explicitly cited in related work) on the same dataset or any shared benchmark. All reported numbers are self-comparisons (ablations) rather than relative to competing methods, making it impossible to assess whether the proposed accuracy/efficiency gains are actually superior to prior art rather than just internally consistent.

Evaluation of band structures is almost entirely qualitative (visual inspection of many band plots) rather than quantitative (e.g., no eigenvalue MAE, k-resolved error statistics beyond the Gauge-MAE on H, or downstream property errors), which weakens the rigor of the central claim of 'DFT-level accuracy' for band structures.

Results are reported for a single training run with a fixed random seed (no variance/error bars across seeds or data splits), so the reliability/stability of the reported Gauge-MAE and ablation deltas is unclear.

The claim of 'universal' generalization is only validated by a single random train/val/test split of similar compounds from Materials Project; there is no evaluation of out-of-distribution generalization (e.g., held-out element groups, unseen structural prototypes, or larger systems than seen in training), despite the paper explicitly highlighting generalization across diverse materials as its core motivation.

The ensemble of four distance-range-specialized sub-models increases training/inference cost and complexity, but there is limited discussion of how this scales with system size or how much of the final accuracy depends on this added complexity versus the core architectural/loss contributions.

Construction cost and scaling of the zeroth-step Hamiltonian H(0) is acknowledged to dominate current runtime and only scale well asymptotically; for the evaluated (non-very-large) test systems the claimed efficiency advantage partly relies on future optimizations not yet implemented, which slightly overstates current practical speedup claims for larger-scale use cases.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated physics-informed input descriptor (the zeroth-step Hamiltonian H(0)) that replaces arbitrary learned atom/edge embeddings, is cheap to compute, and empirically enables good out-of-distribution behavior for an unseen element (Ne) and dramatically shrinks the residual regression target.

Extends the TraceGrad mechanism from a simple GNN backbone to a Transformer architecture with persistent, updated edge features, providing a principled way to combine strict E(3)/O(3) equivariance with non-linear expressiveness for an edge-level (rather than node-level) prediction task.

Provides a rigorous theoretical treatment of the gauge freedom in Hamiltonian regression and of error amplification from the ill-conditioned overlap matrix in reciprocal space, and translates this analysis into a concrete joint R-space/k-space loss with an explicit P-Q decoupling penalty that is shown (via ablations and qualitative band-structure plots) to suppress 'ghost states'.

Curates and releases a large, chemically diverse benchmark dataset (Materials-HAM-SOC: 17,000 structures, 60+ elements, up to f-orbitals, explicit SOC) which fills a real gap in open Hamiltonian-prediction datasets and could be a useful community resource.

Thorough ablation study (Table 4, Appendix L) isolating the contribution of each proposed component (input descriptor, delta-learning target, TraceGrad, ensemble, k-space loss, PQ penalty) with consistent, interpretable trends and qualitative band-structure visualizations across many representative test structures.

Reports a fairly complete efficiency analysis (Table 3) showing large practical speedups over DFT with a sensible breakdown of computational stages, and includes gauge-invariant, element-wise, and downstream-observable (band structure, conductivity) evaluations rather than relying on a single aggregate error metric.
weaknesses: The comparison to prior universal/general Hamiltonian-prediction work is narrow: only DeepH-E3 and the original TraceGrad backbone are directly benchmarked, while other relevant recent universal or broad-coverage models mentioned in related work (e.g., DeepH-2, QHNet, Zhong et al. 2024's universal ML Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian) are discussed qualitatively but never compared quantitatively, making the 'state-of-the-art' and 'universal' claims harder to fully substantiate.

The reported gap versus DeepH-E3 on Materials-HAM-SOC is very large (12.6 meV vs 1.417 meV, ~9x), which is somewhat suspicious given DeepH-E3 is a reasonably mature equivariant method; it is unclear whether DeepH-E3 was tuned/trained to convergence under comparable compute/hyperparameter budgets, raising a fairness concern about baseline strength.

The out-of-distribution generalization claim is supported by a single case study (one Ne-containing structure), which is too limited to substantiate a general claim about extrapolation to unseen elements; the authors themselves acknowledge this is left to future work.

The ensemble-of-4-sub-models design adds noticeable complexity/inference cost (per Appendix I, 4 GPUs are used just for one sample's inference), but the paper does not analyze the accuracy-vs-cost trade-off of the ensemble relative to a single larger model, nor report parameter counts/FLOPs for the full framework versus baselines.

The dataset appears restricted to nonmagnetic compounds and the training pipeline uses a single fixed random seed with no reported variance across runs/splits, limiting confidence in the statistical robustness of the reported gains, especially for the more marginal ablations (e.g., Ablation@Loss-PQ vs Full Method, 1.496 vs 1.417 meV).

Some claims (e.g., 'establish NextHAM as a universal and highly accurate deep learning model') are stated quite strongly in the abstract/conclusion relative to the evidence, which is largely confined to one curated dataset plus two small specialized datasets (MG/MM), rather than external, independently curated benchmarks.

strengths: Introduces a large, diverse benchmark dataset (Materials-HAM-SOC) with 17,000 structures spanning >60 elements and explicit spin-orbit coupling, with high-quality atomic orbital basis sets (up to 4s2p2d1f); this fills a genuine gap since existing open benchmarks (e.g., QH9) are molecular and/or lack SOC and broad elemental coverage.

The zeroth-step Hamiltonian H^(0) as a physically grounded input descriptor (replacing random atom/edge embeddings) is well motivated, cheap to compute (no diagonalization), and the ablation (Table 4) and OOD case study (unseen Ne) provide some evidence of its benefit for generalization.

The k-space (reciprocal-space) loss formulation targeting the P/Q/PQ subspace decoupling is a clear and physically well-motivated contribution that directly addresses the known 'ghost state' error-amplification problem from the ill-conditioned overlap matrix; the ablation and visualized band structures (Fig. 4, Fig. 10) convincingly show its effect.

Rigorous handling of the gauge freedom in Hamiltonian regression (via a gauge-invariant MAE metric and analytically solved gauge parameter), which is a subtle but important methodological detail often overlooked in prior work.

Comprehensive ablation studies (Table 4, Appendix L) isolating the contribution of each proposed component (input descriptor, delta-learning target, TraceGrad, ensemble, k-space loss, PQ penalty), and an efficiency comparison against full DFT workflow (Table 3) showing large wall-clock speedups.
Reasonably strong reproducibility effort: detailed appendices on theory, dataset construction, implementation details, and a stated intent to release code/dataset/models.
weaknesses: Empirical comparison against competing deep-learning methods on the main Materials-HAM-SOC benchmark is limited to a single baseline, DeepH-E3 (Table 5), which the paper itself argues is architecturally weak and not designed for this generalization setting; more recent, directly comparable 'universal' Hamiltonian prediction methods explicitly cited in related work (e.g., Wang et al. 2024c 'Universal materials model of deep-learning DFT Hamiltonian', DeepH-2, QHNet/Yu et al.) are discussed but never quantitatively benchmarked on the new dataset, leaving the central claim of state-of-the-art universal performance only partially substantiated.

The out-of-distribution generalization claim (Section 4.2) rests on a single unseen element (Ne) and a single structure, which is too limited a test to support general claims about generalization to unseen chemistries; the authors themselves acknowledge this needs 'further element-level out-of-distribution evaluations' in future work.

The TraceGrad/Transformer comparison against the original TraceGrad work is only performed on a 'cut-down' version of NextHAM on small specialized datasets (Monolayer Graphene/MoS2, Table 7), not on the main large-scale SOC benchmark, making it hard to assess how much of the improvement on the primary benchmark stems from the proposed Transformer extension versus other components.

Results show noticeably uneven error distribution across Hamiltonian blocks: the real part of the spin-conserving (↑↑/↓↓) blocks retains a much larger Gauge MAE (2.834 meV) than the spin-flip blocks (<0.001 meV), yet the abstract's headline claim of 'sub-μeV scale' accuracy could be read as applying more broadly than it does, which risks overstating the main result.

No uncertainty/variance reporting (single training run with fixed seed), no parameter/compute-cost accounting for the 4-submodel ensemble beyond inference time, and no discussion of training cost, which limits assessment of practical overhead and robustness of the reported gains.

The method combines several previously proposed components (Equiformer backbone, TraceGrad, delta-learning, Wigner-Eckart decoding) with incremental architectural extensions; the degree of genuine methodological novelty beyond integration and the k-space ghost-state loss is moderate.

The per-element error map (Fig. 3) and band-structure case studies are presented qualitatively without aggregated quantitative error statistics (e.g., band-structure MAE averaged over the full test set), making it harder to judge the overall reliability of downstream physical quantities beyond the handful of illustrated examples.

The manuscript is extremely dense and heavily appendix-reliant (44 pages), which, combined with the limited baseline comparisons, makes it difficult for readers to evaluate how the method would fare against the broader current state of the art in a more standardized setting.
